title: The Crucifixion Question
subtitle: The historical case, the Quranic denial, and why Muslims trust revelation
summary: The earliest Christian sources present Jesus as crucified, and most historians accept that a crucifixion occurred. The Quran nevertheless states that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified, but that it was made to appear so, and that God raised him. Islam does not deny the evidence carelessly; it distinguishes what historical methods can infer from surviving reports from what reliable revelation can disclose about an exceptional event.

sections.title: Why Muslims Reject the Crucifixion of Jesus
sections.body: Most historians accept a crucifixion because Paul's letters and the Gospels are early sources that say it occurred. Muslims acknowledge that evidence while trusting the Quran's explicit correction: Jesus was not killed or crucified, and God raised him. The real issue is therefore whether the Quran is revelation and can correct a conclusion based on human testimony.

sections.title: A Major Point of Disagreement
sections.body: The cross stands at the center of mainstream Christianity. Islam honors Jesus as Messiah and mighty messenger but denies that his enemies killed him. A responsible Muslim case neither invents a detailed substitute story nor pretends that Christian sources say nothing about crucifixion. It states both records clearly and asks which source carries final authority.

sections.title: History and Revelation Answer Different Questions
sections.body: Historical study weighs surviving documents and usually selects the explanation that best fits ordinary experience. It cannot directly observe first-century events or rule out divine intervention as a matter of method. Revelation makes a different claim: the God who knows the event tells humanity what truly occurred. Trusting that correction depends on the wider case for the Quran, not on pretending the historical evidence is absent.

sections.title: What Historians Commonly Conclude
sections.body: Paul's letters refer to Jesus's death, and all four canonical Gospels narrate a crucifixion. Later non-Christian references are brief and do not provide independent eyewitness detail, but they reflect the public Christian claim. For these reasons, most historians regard a Roman crucifixion as highly probable. That consensus deserves accurate representation, even though historical probability is not the same as revelation-based certainty.

sections.title: The Quran's Clear Correction
sections.body:
The Quran states:

وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ فِيهِ لَفِى شَكٍّۢ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًۢا

'They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but it was made to appear so to them ... They did not kill him for certain' (Quran 4:157). The next verse says:

بَل رَّفَعَهُ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ ۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًۭا

'Rather, Allah raised him to Himself. And Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise' (4:158).

The Quran does not name another person, describe the precise mechanism, or authorize certainty about details it leaves unstated. Its central affirmations are clear: Jesus's enemies did not succeed, and God raised His messenger.

sections.title: What the New Testament Affirms
sections.body: The Gospels narrate Jesus's arrest, trial, crucifixion, burial, and appearances after death. Paul writes that Christ died and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Christians interpret these claims as the saving center of the Gospel. The accounts also contain differences in chronology and detail, but the broad crucifixion claim is common to them and should not be hidden.

sections.title: Where the Evidence Leads
sections.body: If the New Testament is treated as the final authority, the Christian conclusion follows. If the Quran is established as God's final revelation, its correction takes priority over human reports. The Islamic case rests on the Quran's preservation, message of uncompromising monotheism, fulfilled signs, and coherence—not on one isolated attempt to disprove every historical argument for crucifixion.

sections.title: What the Muslim Position Does and Does Not Claim
sections.body: Islam does not teach that Jesus deserved death, that his mission failed, or that his enemies defeated him. It does not require one particular substitute theory. It also does not depend on dismissing every historian as biased. It says that ordinary historical reconstruction reached an understandable conclusion from available reports, while God revealed that the apparent outcome was not the final reality.

sections.title: Honor Without Atonement
sections.body: In Islam, God saved and raised Jesus; He did not abandon His messenger or require his blood before forgiving others. Every soul bears its own responsibility, and every sinner may repent directly to God. This preserves Jesus's honor, God's justice, and the prophetic call to worship the Creator rather than a crucified creation.

sections.title: The Central Takeaway
sections.body: The crucifixion question ultimately returns to revelation. Historical sources explain why crucifixion became the dominant human account. The Quran provides a direct divine correction and calls people back to the one God worshiped by Jesus.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus was crucified?
A: No. The Quran states that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified but that it was made to appear so (4:157), and that God raised him to Himself (4:158). Muslims receive this as God's direct testimony.

Q: If it was not Jesus on the cross, who was it?
A: The Quran does not say. Many classical commentators spoke of a substitute made to resemble Jesus, but no identification is part of the Quranic text or required belief. Muslims are content to leave the mechanism with God.

Q: Don't historians agree the crucifixion happened?
A: Mainstream scholarship does regard it as among the best-attested facts of Jesus' life, and Muslims should acknowledge that honestly. But historical method excludes divine intervention by design, while the Quran's claim is precisely that God intervened in what observers perceived. The same method also declines to affirm the resurrection — so both faiths ultimately rest on revelation at the decisive point.

Q: Without the cross, how are sins forgiven in Islam?
A: Directly. The sinner repents sincerely and God forgives out of His mercy — no intermediary, no sacrifice, no transferred guilt, for no soul bears the burden of another (Quran 35:18).

Q: Is Jesus alive now, according to Islam?
A: The majority view is that God raised him alive and that he will return before the Day of Resurrection — a hope described in reports including Sahih al-Bukhari 2476 and Sahih Muslim 2937a, and connected by most commentators to Quran 4:159.

Q: Does denying the crucifixion dishonor Jesus?
A: The opposite. In the Islamic account the denial is God's rescue and vindication of a beloved messenger, whom Muslims may never mention except with reverence.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **The Crucifixion and the Qur'an: A Study in the History of Muslim Thought** — Todd Lawson. A scholarly survey of how Muslim commentators across the centuries have interpreted Quran 4:157, showing the range of readings from substitution to appearance.
- **Christ in Islam and Christianity** — Neal Robinson. A careful academic comparison of the Jesus of the Quran and classical Muslim exegesis with the Jesus of Christian doctrine, including the crucifixion passages.
- **Jesus in the Qur'an** — Geoffrey Parrinder. A classic, sympathetic study of every Quranic passage about Jesus, written by a scholar of comparative religion and accessible to beginners.
- **The Muslim Jesus: Sayings and Stories in Islamic Literature** — Tarif Khalidi. A collection showing the deep reverence for Jesus within the Islamic tradition beyond the Quran itself.
- **Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium** — Bart D. Ehrman. A reconstruction of the historical Jesus by a prominent non-Christian historian — useful for seeing how the secular historical case for the crucifixion is actually argued.

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا ٱلْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ فِيهِ لَفِى شَكٍّۢ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًۢا
quranVerses.translation: And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: بَل رَّفَعَهُ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ ۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًۭا
quranVerses.translation: Rather, Allah raised him to Himself. And ever is Allah Exalted in Might and Wise.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَإِن مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ إِلَّا لَيُؤْمِنَنَّ بِهِۦ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِۦ ۖ وَيَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ يَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًۭا
quranVerses.translation: And there is none from the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in Jesus before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَىٰٓ إِنِّى مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَىَّ وَمُطَهِّرُكَ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ وَجَاعِلُ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوكَ فَوْقَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ ۖ ثُمَّ إِلَىَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَأَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ فِيمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ
quranVerses.translation: [Mention] when Allah said, "O Jesus, indeed I will take you and raise you to Myself and purify you from those who disbelieve and make those who follow you [in submission to Allah alone] superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that in which you used to differ.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌۭ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ ۚ وَإِن تَدْعُ مُثْقَلَةٌ إِلَىٰ حِمْلِهَا لَا يُحْمَلْ مِنْهُ شَىْءٌۭ وَلَوْ كَانَ ذَا قُرْبَىٰٓ ۗ إِنَّمَا تُنذِرُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُم بِٱلْغَيْبِ وَأَقَامُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ ۚ وَمَن تَزَكَّىٰ فَإِنَّمَا يَتَزَكَّىٰ لِنَفْسِهِۦ ۚ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلْمَصِيرُ
quranVerses.translation: And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls [another] to [carry some of] its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he should be a close relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and have established prayer. And whoever purifies himself only purifies himself for [the benefit of] his soul. And to Allah is the [final] destination.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
It was the third hour, and they crucified him.
About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?” That is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
He said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire.”

faq.question: Do Muslims believe Jesus was crucified?
faq.answer: No. Quran 4:157 states that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified and 4:158 states that God raised him.

faq.question: If it was not Jesus on the cross, who was it?
faq.answer: The Quran does not identify another person. Specific substitute stories are interpretations, not explicit Quranic teaching.

faq.question: Don't historians agree the crucifixion happened?
faq.answer: Most do, based mainly on early Christian sources. Islam acknowledges that historical judgment but gives final authority to revelation from the God who knows the event directly.

faq.question: Without the cross, how are sins forgiven in Islam?
faq.answer: Through sincere repentance and God's mercy. Islam rejects transferred guilt and teaches that no soul bears another's burden.

faq.question: Is Jesus alive now, according to Islam?
faq.answer: Islam teaches that God raised Jesus and that he will return before the end of time. Details are established from authentic revelation, not speculation.

faq.question: Does denying the crucifixion dishonor Jesus?
faq.answer: No. The Quran presents it as God's vindication of Jesus and the failure of his enemies to destroy him.
